newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan passes state oil firm budget with cuts.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan passes state oil firm budget with cuts.

text.p: After months of delay, Taiwan's parliament on Thursday adopted state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp's fiscal 1996-97 budget, but only after cutting funding for projects in Vietnam and Indonesia, officials said.

There was no immediate word as to whether the parliament would act on Chinese Petroleum's proposal to raise domestic petrol prices by up to 10 percent, although action could be taken before the end of Thursday's session, they said.

Parliament cut funding for a plan to move the company's Number 2 naphtha cracker to Indonesia and for its plan to build a small power plant at Taoyuan south of the Taiwan capital Taipei, vice president Roy Chiu told Reuters by telephone.
Parliament cancelled funding for Chinese Petroleum's plan to cooperate with Vietnam in a proposed US$16 million solvent production plant, Chiu said.
Chinese Petroleum president Pan Wen-yen has vowed to cancel the plan to move its mothballed No.2 cracker to Indonesia if it could not finalise a site for the plant by February.

Parliament added T$2.5 billion to Chinese Petroleum's fiscal year income to bring total budgeted income to T$341.36 billion and set total budgeted expenses to T$320.86 billion, resulting in a budgeted profit of T$20.5 billion, officials said.
The profit figure becomes the base against which the company will have to adjust its petroleum prices, officials said.
The state monopoly, which cannot adjust prices more than three percent a month without state approval, has petitioned the economics ministry to permit an unspecified increase.
Company sources say it wants a hike of up to 10 percent.
Chinese Petroleum's operations already have fallen into the red due to higher-than-budgeted world oil prices.
It reported a deficit of T$8.126 billion for July-November.

The new budget, retroactive to the current fiscal year's July 1 start, had been stalled for months as lawmakers debated the merits of the monopoly's ambitious privatisation plan, which was to have begun in 1996 with a public stock issue.

Company executives have warned that delays and possibly hasty reschedulings increased the risk of a disorderly privatisation that could result in control of the strategically important company falling into the hands of small but powerful interests, rather than the wider public as hoped.
The freeze was led by ruling Nationalist Party lawmakers in the interest of better oil industry regulation and a more careful assessment of Chinese Petroleum's market value.

Chinese Petroleum had proposed holding a 10 percent stake in the T$18 billion (US$650 million), 900 megawatt Taoyuan power plant project, which is likely to be built anyway by a consortium led by Ever Fortune Industrial Co.
